PART 1. The problem

1.1 The problem, stated with what the code shows

NXERP puts several applications behind one login. After login, /nxerp/go and /nxerp/apps use role grants to decide which app a user may open. That part works, and it is not the problem. RBAC (role-based access control) is already implemented and clear. It stays.

The problem is the shared database. The apps run in the same Frappe process on the same site, so they use one database and one database login. RBAC checks who the user is. It cannot restrict what the code can read, because every RBAC check (has_permission, permission_query_conditions, the launcher) is Python running inside the same process as that one database connection.

Consequence (JUDGMENT, resting on the FACTs in 1.2): an injection bug, a vulnerable dependency, or a badly written report or API in the internet-facing Helpdesk gives an attacker the one database login of the site. That login can read every app's tables, including ERPNext's accounting, employee and operational records. Hiding an icon, or the nxerp gate, does not change that, because a flaw that runs SQL or Python bypasses Frappe's permission checks.

This setup has an established name: the Shared Database or Integration Database pattern, which architects advise avoiding (Section 3, sources S3 and S9). The fix, in Part 2, is the Database per Application pattern.

Be precise about what is not wrong today (FACT): none of Helpdesk's raw SQL touches ERPNext tables. Helpdesk has 8 frappe.db.sql calls outside patches and tests, all on tabHD Ticket or tabCommunication or install-time indexes (for example apps/helpdesk/helpdesk/helpdesk/doctype/hd_ticket/hd_ticket.py:1484, apps/helpdesk/helpdesk/helpdesk/report/ticket_summary/ticket_summary.py:343). The risk is the capability of the shared account, not a known misuse.

PART 2. The analysis

Section 1. Solution: remove the shared database

1.1 What already works, and what the real problem is

You already have RBAC (role-based access control) and it is clear and working. It stays. The problem is a different layer, and it is the shared database.

LayerQuestion it answersStatusWhat we do
Authentication (login)Who are you?Works (Frappe /login)Keep
Authorization, RBACWhat may this user open or change?Works (roles, DocType permissions, the nxerp gate, apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/enforcement.py)Keep, unchanged
Application visibilityWhich apps do you see?Works (launcher, router)Keep
Data storageWhere does each app's data live, and who can reach it?PROBLEM: one shared database, one shared database loginFix: this is the whole point of this plan

Why RBAC cannot fix the data layer: RBAC is a check written in application code. It answers "may this user do this?". It cannot answer "which tables can this code reach?". Because every app runs with the same database login, any flaw in any app (an injection bug, a vulnerable library, a badly written report) bypasses RBAC and sees every table. The database itself has no wall.

This problem has an established name. It is the Shared Database pattern, also called the Integration Database, and it is documented as something to avoid. Martin Fowler: "integration databases should be avoided" because "the database becomes a point of coupling between the applications that access it." (EVIDENCE, Section 3, source S3.) microservices.io lists its costs: schema changes must be coordinated across teams, and "all services access the same database [so] they can potentially interfere with one another" (EVIDENCE, S9).

1.2 The solution in one sentence

Give every application its own database and its own database login (the "Database per Application" pattern), keep RBAC and the one login on top, and let applications exchange data only through APIs and events, never through the database.

1.3 How the solution fixes the shared database, in the database itself

Shared-database problem today (FACT, Part 1)What changes in the database layer
One database holds every app's tables side by side (and every new app would add more)One database per app, plus the identity database: three today (identity, Helpdesk, ERPNext), six with the three planned apps. An app's tables exist only in its own database.
One database login can read and write all of themOne login per database, allowed on that database only. Helpdesk's login cannot even see ERPNext's database.
Helpdesk code reads and writes ERPNext's Customer table directly (apps/helpdesk/helpdesk/hooks.py:82-88)No cross-database access at all. Helpdesk keeps a small copy of customer names in its own database and asks ERPNext's API for details.
One shared user tableOne master user table (identity database), copied without passwords to each app's own database
One backup and one restore for everythingOne backup and restore per database
A schema change in one app can break anotherEach app migrates only its own database; the API between apps is versioned
Finance data and an internet-facing app on one database serverERPNext's database on its own server

StepWhat we do (plain words)Phase

Section 2. Chosen architecture

2.1 The selected architecture, by name

Selected architectureDatabase per Application (the "Database per Service" pattern applied to NXERP's applications), also called siloed data or shared-nothing data ownership
Database sharingNo. UNSHARED. Each application has its own database and its own database login. No shared tables, no shared schema, no shared database account, no cross-database query.
Database server sharingPartly, and that is allowed. Databases of normal business data (identity, Helpdesk, and later Project Management) are separate databases on one "standard" MariaDB server. Databases of finance and HR data (ERPNext, and later HRMS and Budget) are separate databases on a second, "restricted" server. Within a server every database has its own login. Microsoft's guidance: "Services can safely share the same physical database server. Problems occur when services share the same schema, or they read and write to the same set of database tables." (EVIDENCE, S2)
The one shared thingThe login, not a database: Federated Identity / Single Sign-On (OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow, as in OpenID Connect). The identity site's database holds only users and access grants.
How apps exchange dataAPI with published versioned contracts (reads) and event-carried state transfer (signed webhooks that keep a small local copy). Never database access.
Overall isolation styleThe Bridge model (AWS SaaS Lens): the data tier is siloed per application; identity and operations are shared.
AuthorizationRBAC, unchanged, now running inside each application.

The four levels of database sharing, and where each part of NXERP sits:

LevelDescriptionUsed by
0Shared tables, one database, one login (the Integration Database)Today, all apps (we leave this)
1Separate databases and separate logins on one serverChosen inside each tier: identity, Helpdesk and Project Management on the standard server; ERPNext, HRMS and Budget on the restricted server
2Separate database serversChosen between the two tiers: finance and HR data never share a server with the rest
3Separate machinesFuture option when a trigger in 2.10 is met

Scope: this is built for five applications, not two. Two applications are installed today. Three more are planned, and the design treats every application the same way.

Engine. The database engine stays MariaDB 11.8 (ADR-002). The pattern is the same on PostgreSQL (separate databases, one role each, CONNECT revoked from PUBLIC), but changing engine is not part of this plan.

Prerequisite. This design needs separate databases and logins to exist. If only one database and one login are allowed, it cannot be delivered (Section 5).

Planned apps appear in every diagram with a dashed outline and the word "planned". Nothing is built, installed or shown to users for them (the repository rule in CLAUDE.md); the design only guarantees that adding each one repeats the same short routine (Section 2.8) and touches no existing app.

2.3 The decision, in the standard decision-record format

PartContent
ContextFACT: six apps share one site, one database and one database login (Part 1). RBAC works, but it cannot limit what code can read. A flaw in the internet-facing Helpdesk reaches every table.
DecisionJUDGMENT: adopt Database per Application. Add a federated identity site. Put ERPNext's database on a separate server. Exchange data only by versioned APIs and signed events.
ConsequencesA flaw in Helpdesk exposes only Helpdesk's database. There are more things to run (three sites, two database servers). Helpdesk can no longer write into ERPNext. Backups, restores and schema changes become per application.
Alternatives consideredSection 2.11.

2.4 The system: the full picture first, then simpler views

The full picture. Read it from top to bottom: each horizontal band is a layer, and each column is a site. Bold arrows are database logins (one per site). Thin lines are caches and files. Dashed arrows between sites are the only app-to-app channels (A = access grants, C = a read-only contract). Dashed outlines are planned apps (3 to 5). The columns are grouped by database tier, so the two database servers sit side by side. The picture is generated from the list of apps, so adding an app adds a column. Notice what repeats for every app: its own site, its own Redis cache and queue, its own database and login, its own files volume.

Life of a request through the layers (the numbered circles on the Helpdesk column of the picture):

#StepLayerWhat happens
1A user opens a web addressAccessHTTPS reaches the host proxy, then the edge proxy
2The edge routes by addressAccess to applicationthe request goes to that app's site only
3The app checks accessApplicationthe RBAC gate: signed in, enabled, has the role for this app
4The app checks its own cacheCache and queueits own Redis cache; no other app's cache is reachable
5The app reads or writes its dataDatabaseswith its own login, on its own database only
6The app reads or stores filesFiles and secretsits own volume
7Slow work is queuedCache and queuea job in the app's own Redis queue; its own worker runs it and writes to its own database

RuleHow it is enforced
A login works only on its own databaseFrappe's GRANT ... ON <db>.* (database level, no *.*) plus the login is allowed only from that stack's network range (--mariadb-user-host-login-scope)

ERPNext database (owned by the ERPNext site; relevant tables only)

Every planned app repeats this pattern. A future app's database holds its own business tables, a copy of the users (no passwords) with their roles, and, only where a contract exists, a small local copy of another app's record with that record's plain ID.

What links the databases? Not foreign keys, and not queries. Only identifiers stored as plain values and resolved through an API:

Who owns each kind of data (single source of truth)

DataOwnerStored inEveryone else gets it by
Users, passwords, 2FA secretsidentity siteidentity databasea copy of the user (no password) pushed to each app
"May open Helpdesk or ERPNext"identity siteidentity database (a role)the same role copied to the app's user
Customer master, invoices, ledgerERPNext siteERPNext databaseHelpdesk: read-only API and a signed-event mirror
Customer name and type, as seen by HelpdeskERPNext (source), Helpdesk keeps a copyHelpdesk database (HD Customer)n/a
Tickets, messages, attachments, SLAsHelpdesk siteHelpdesk databasenobody
Employees, leave, payroll (planned)HRMS siteHRMS databaseother apps only through a registered read-only contract
Projects and tasks (planned)Project Management siteProject Management databasesame
Budgets and approvals (planned)Budget siteBudget databasesame

Note: Frappe creates its core tables (User, Contact, Communication, File) in every database. They have the same names and different rows in each database; none of them is shared.

2.7 How data flows, end to end

The big picture: a data-flow diagram. Rounded shapes are people and outside systems, boxes are processes, and cylinders are the three databases. A process reads and writes only its own site's database. Flows between sites go from process to process, over an API (bold arrows A, C, D, E; dashed arrow B). The dashed box is the same pattern repeated for each planned app. There is no arrow from any process to another site's database, because no such path exists.

Flow 1. Give someone access to an app (shown for any app: Helpdesk, ERPNext or a planned one). The change is written in the identity database, queued, and delivered to the Helpdesk database through the Helpdesk site's API.

Flow 2. Sign in once, open any app. The password is checked only against the identity database. That app's database is asked only "is this user enabled here, with which roles?"

Flow 3. A customer emails support. Everything stays inside the Helpdesk database. No other database is touched.

Flow 4. An agent opens a ticket and needs customer details from ERPNext. The only cross-application read today, and it goes through an API. Any future pair of apps would follow this same pattern, and only after a contract is registered (the matrix in 2.8).

If ERPNext is down, step 5 fails and the agent sees the customer name from the local copy, with a note. No ticket is lost.

Flow 5. A customer is created or changed in ERPNext. ERPNext announces the change; Helpdesk updates its own copy. Helpdesk never writes to ERPNext.

Flow 6. A new app joins (apps 3 to 5, and any later app). This is how the design stays cheap to extend: the same few steps, and nothing existing changes.

Summary of the six flows: what is read and written where

FlowReads fromWrites toCrosses a database boundary?
1 Grant accessidentity databaseidentity database (role, outbox), then Helpdesk database (user, role)Yes, by API only, never by a database connection
2 Sign inidentity database, Helpdesk databaseidentity cache, Helpdesk cacheYes, "who is this?" by API
3 Ticket from emailHelpdesk databaseHelpdesk databaseNo
4 Customer detailsHelpdesk database, ERPNext databaseHelpdesk cacheYes, one read-only API call
5 Customer changedERPNext databaseERPNext database, then Helpdesk database (the copy)Yes, signed message
6 A new app joinsidentity database (register the app)the new app's own database and files, and the identity database (the Peer row)No existing database is touched

Backups follow the same boundaries. Each database gets its own encrypted backup and its own restore. Restoring Helpdesk never touches ERPNext (Phase 1 and Section 6).

The routine is the same for every app, and no existing app, database, cache or login is touched. (Flow 6 in 2.7 shows it as a picture.)

What each app gets, and what is shared

Each app has its own (never shared)Shared by all apps
site and web address; database and database login; Redis cache; Redis queue; background worker; scheduler; websocket; files and secrets volume; backup job; NXERP Peer record; OAuth client; registry entrythe edge proxy; the identity site; a database server within its tier (not a database); the host machine

Footprint: what it costs as apps are added. A site runs 6 long-running containers (web, websocket, worker, scheduler, Redis cache, Redis queue; FACT: the services in deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml). These counts are JUDGMENT (arithmetic from that file):

The cost grows in a straight line, about 6 containers and 1 database per app. The sources say the same: the pattern trades more things to run for isolation and loose coupling (S1, S11). If memory becomes a problem the answer is container limits first, and only later a bigger host or an extra machine (2.10). Do not share Redis between apps to save memory: that is how the cache layer stops being a boundary.

2.10 When an app should move to stronger separation

LevelMove an app here when
1: own database on the standard server (default)normal business data. In this plan: identity, Helpdesk, Project Management
2: the restricted serverit holds payroll, tax, bank or other regulated data, or is internet-facing and holds finance data, or needs a different restore time. In this plan: ERPNext now; HRMS (employee data) and Budget Management (finance) when they arrive

Section 3. Proof: where this architecture is used in the real world

This section answers one question: is "Database per Application, with one federated login and API-only integration" a real, proven approach, used to solve the same kind of problem? Every source below was opened on 2026-11-03. I say what each source actually says, who published it, and how strong it is as proof. Where evidence is thin I say so (3.4).

3.1 What is being proven

ClaimMeaning
AGiving each application its own private database (instead of sharing one) is the standard, documented answer to the shared-database problem.
BIt works together with one shared login: you do not need a shared database to have single sign-on.
CApplications should exchange data through APIs and events, not through each other's tables.
DTwo databases on the same server is acceptable, as long as they do not share schemas or tables.
EThe shared database is the recognised problem, and the cause of the symptoms in Part 1.
FThe pattern scales to many applications (we plan five, and more later), with a cost that grows per application.

3.2 The real-world evidence

IDWho and what, and where I read itWhat it actually says or doesMatches our designStrength
S1Amazon Web Services, Prescriptive Guidance: "Database-per-service pattern" Source: docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/modernization-data-persistence/database-per-service.htmlMicroservices "don't share a data layer"; "individual data stores cannot be directly accessed by other microservices, and persistent data is accessed only by APIs"; use it when services "have different compliance or security requirements for their databases"; IAM policies "ensure that data is kept private". Costs: queries that span services are hard; you manage several databases; you need API composition, CQRS or event sourcing for cross-service queries.A, C; least privilege; our API window and mirrorOfficial vendor guidance
S2Microsoft, Azure Architecture Center: "Data considerations for microservices" Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/microservices/design/data-considerations"Two services shouldn't share a data store. Each service manages its own private data store, and other services can't access it directly." The rule prevents coupling through shared schemas. "Services can safely share the same physical database server. Problems occur when services share the same schema, or they read and write to the same set of database tables." Use "a single source of truth"; other services may hold their own eventually consistent copy; use events to build a materialized view.A, C, D; our standard server; single owner per data; the customer copy in HelpdeskOfficial vendor guidance
S3Martin Fowler (ThoughtWorks), bliki: "Integration Database" Source: martinfowler.com/bliki/IntegrationDatabase.html"integration databases should be avoided"; "the database becomes a point of coupling between the applications that access it"; this "significantly increases the risk involved in changing those applications".E; names today's setupRespected practitioner
S4Martin Fowler and James Lewis, "Microservices" Source: martinfowler.com/articles/microservices.htmlEnterprises often share one database across many applications, frequently for licensing reasons; "Microservices prefer letting each service manage its own database", as separate instances of the same technology or another system. Consistency across services is usually eventual.A, ERespected practitioners (the section heading was partly cut in the copy I read)
S5Microsoft, Power Platform: "Environments overview" (Dataverse) Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/admin/environments-overviewAn environment is "a container to separate apps that might have different roles, security requirements, or target audiences". S6Shopify Engineering: "A Pods Architecture To Allow Shopify To Scale" Source: shopify.engineering/a-pods-architecture-to-allow-shopify-to-scaleAfter sharding they "needed to fully isolate each shard so a failure couldn't spiral out into a platform outage." "A pod consists of a set of shops that live on a fully isolated set of datastores." Shared resources "can only ever communicate to a single pod at a time. Job workers, app servers and load balancers stay shared.A; the blast-radius reason; a shared layer over isolated dataThe company's own design claim (not independent)
S7Martin Fowler, "What do you mean by Event-Driven?" Source: martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.htmlEvent-carried State Transfer: update clients "in such a way that they don't need to contact the source system"; "What we gain is greater resilience, since the recipient systems can function." Down-side: "lots of data schlepped around and lots of copies."C; our signed-event customer copy in HelpdeskRespected practitioner
S8OpenID Foundation, "OpenID Connect Core 1.0" Source: openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html"a simple identity layer on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol." S9Chris Richardson, microservices.io: "Shared database" pattern Source: microservices.io/patterns/data/shared-database.htmlOne database shared by services where each "freely accesses data owned by other services using local ACID transactions." S10microservices.io: "API Composition" Source: microservices.io/patterns/data/api-composition.htmlOnce each service has its own database, "it is no longer straightforward to implement queries that join data from multiple services"; the answer is an API composer that calls each owner and joins in memory. 3.3 How the evidence supports each claim

ClaimSourcesVerdict
A. Database per application is the standard answerS1, S2, S4, S5, S6, S11, S13, S14Strongly supported: official guidance from two major cloud vendors, a product platform, a large company design, and the framework you already run
B. It works with one shared loginS5, S8, S12Supported: Dataverse (silo databases under one Entra tenant), the SaaS Lens ("a silo still relies on a shared identity") and the OpenID Connect standard
C. Exchange data through APIs and eventsS1, S2, S7, S10Supported
D. Same server is fine, shared schema is notS2, S11Supported by one official source and one practitioner source; our restricted ERPNext server follows S11's "server per service"
E. The shared database is the recognised problemS3, S4, S9Supported
F. It scales to many appsS1, S2, S6, S11Supported, with a stated cost: the sources describe the pattern for any number of services and Shopify runs many isolated pods; they also name the cost (more databases to operate, harder cross-app queries), which Section 2.8 quantifies for five apps

3.4 Where the evidence is thin, and what does not transfer

  • Most sources are about microservices and cloud services, not ERPs on Frappe. ERP-class evidence is thinner: Frappe itself (S14), Odoo (S15, weak) and Power Platform (S5). I did not open SAP, Oracle or Dynamics 365 material.
  • Vendor documents and company blogs are design claims, not proof of outcomes. S1, S2, S5, S6, S12 and S13 say what to do and why; none gives failure statistics.
  • The sources prove the pattern, not our implementation. Section 3.5 gives the tests that prove it for NXERP.
  • The pattern has costs (S1, S9, S10, S11): joining data across applications is harder and you run more databases. We accept that and use API composition (S10) and a small event-fed copy (S7).
  • Not used, because they did not support a claim: the Atlassian Jira database page (opened, states no rule about separate databases), the AWS "Implementing Microservices on AWS" page (returned only a title), Frappe Cloud isolation claims (marketing or snippet only).
  • Not researched: Amazon's and Netflix's internal practice, secrets managers, the OAuth security best-current-practice document, and the Kubernetes sandboxing sections (the page was cut off).

Section 6. Production data migration and rollback

Approach (JUDGMENT): extract and load per app with a short freeze; no dual-run. The only two-way write path between Helpdesk and ERPNext is the feature being removed; Frappe has no multi-master replication, so dual-run would need a hand-built two-way sync of tickets, emails and files. Which app moves first: Helpdesk and identity are extracted from the existing site; the existing site keeps serving ERPNext (as the interim erp site, attached to the identity site) until M6, when its data is restored into the new erp stack on the restricted instance. ERPNext holds the larger and more sensitive data, so its site stays untouched until the new topology has proven itself. How Helpdesk is extracted: restore a full backup of the live site into the new hd site, then run bench --site hd.<domain> uninstall-app erpnext (and payments) and prune orphaned core rows. Frappe has no per-app export, so this keeps record names, creation and modified stamps, Versions, comments, assignments, email threads (Communication), attachments (File rows plus the file tree) and Dynamic Link rows exactly (UNRESOLVED until rehearsed). How id is built: a fresh site with nxerp only, then an identity-only copy of User, Has Role, Role, Role Profile and the user rows of __Auth (password hashes and 2FA secrets), so logins and 2FA keep working without a forced reset (UNRESOLVED: __Auth layout in v16.53.0 to confirm). Users on the app sites keep their rows (ownership and audit links need them); the identity site is the source of truth for who is enabled.

The same movement as a picture: the old database is never changed until step 6, which is why rollback is real until the decision point D.

Rollback is real only because the original site is untouched until D. Reverting code does not reverse database changes, so rollback means pointing users back at a database that was never modified, plus replaying writes made elsewhere.

D = the earlier of 7 days after opening to customers or the owner's sign-off after one full business cycle, always preceded by RP-final (full backups of erp and hd, restore drill passed). Restore points: RP0 (source at T0), RP1 (hd after prune), RP2 (daily on hd), RP-final (before M5), RP-erp (before M6). Divergent writes exist only between the canary and D; the delta tool (NEW nxerp/cutover.py) handles them and is a hard prerequisite of M4.

PART 3. Implementation phases

How the work is built, and where

Changes are additive and off by default: new environments are built next to the old stack, and each new behaviour is switched on by a site setting (nxerp_site_role, nxerp_bridge_mode, nxerp_cutover_allowed), so merging code does not change production. Each prompt is one branch and one pull request. Platform code goes in apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/, Helpdesk code only in Helpdesk's own integration files, deployment in deploy/. Section 4.1 lists the eight rules and Section 4.2 maps every area of the repository to the phases that touch it.

What Claude Code can do, and what only you can do

One prompt per phase is not enough, and it is not the only work. Each phase below has several short prompts (17 in total). One prompt is one sitting and one pull request; run them in order, and read each report before the next.

Claude Code canClaude Code cannot

write tests and run them on a dev site, if Docker is available therecreate DNS records or certificates
write runbooks, decision records and checklistshold or create your real passwords and keys
create branches and commits (never push or merge unless you ask)take a production backup or touch production
research and read Frappe source in the benchchoose a maintenance window, or make business choices

So every phase has two kinds of work, shown in different boxes: PROMPTS (Claude Code does it) and WHAT I MUST DO MYSELF (you do it, with exact commands).

How to run a phase

  1. Open the phase tab. Read Part 1 (goal and done-when) and the At a glance table.
  2. Paste the prompts one at a time, in order, into Claude Code. Each one stops by itself and reports. If it says a step needs you, it writes it under USER-ACTION-REQUIRED.
  3. Do What I must do myself while or after the prompts run.
  4. Check the verification list in Part 8. Only then start the next phase.
  5. If something goes wrong, use the rollback in Part 8 of that phase.

Glossary (terms you will meet in the steps)

TermMeaning
Docker / container / imageDocker runs programs in isolated boxes called containers. An image is the frozen recipe a container starts from.
Docker Compose / project / serviceCompose starts several containers from one YAML file. A project is one running copy of that file (named with -p); a service is one container definition inside it.
VolumeStorage that survives when a container is deleted. docker compose down -v deletes volumes, and with them the data.
Docker network, internalA private virtual network between containers. An internal network has no route to the outside world. Two containers talk only if they share a network.
Frappe site / benchA site is one Frappe installation with its own database. A bench is the folder that holds Frappe's code and many sites. bench is the command-line tool.
MariaDB, database, account, rootMariaDB is the database server. A database holds tables. An account is a login with listed rights. Root is the all-powerful account; its password must never sit in an app container.
GrantA right given to an account, for example "everything on database X and nothing else". SHOW GRANTS lists them.
RedisA fast in-memory store Frappe uses for cache, background-job queues and live updates.
Reverse proxy / edgeA web server in front of the apps that receives all browser traffic and forwards it to the right app by host name. Here: nginx.
DNS A recordA public entry that maps a name such as id.example.test to your server's IP address.
TLS certificate / HTTPSThe file that lets browsers talk to your server encrypted. Let's Encrypt issues them free with the certbot tool.
Environment file (.env)A text file of NAME=value lines holding passwords. Never commit it; set permission 600 (only you can read it).
SecretAny password, key or token. Generate with python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(24))'.
ageA small free tool that encrypts files with a public key; only the matching private key opens them.
Backup, restore, restore drillA backup is a copy; a restore puts it back; a drill proves the restore works by doing it on a scratch copy.
OAuth / SSO / Social Login KeyOAuth lets one site vouch for a user to another. SSO means signing in once. In Frappe, a Social Login Key is the setting that tells a site to accept logins from another provider.
API key and secret / tokenA pair that lets a program (not a person) call Frappe's API; sent as Authorization: token key:secret.
Webhook / HMACA webhook is a message one system posts to another when something changes. HMAC is a signature computed with a shared secret so the receiver can reject forgeries.
Provisioning / reconcileProvisioning creates or disables a user on another site. Reconcile compares both sides and repairs differences.
Maintenance modeA Frappe site setting that answers "under maintenance" instead of serving users.
Freeze window, canaryA freeze window is a short agreed period when nobody writes. A canary is a first small group (here: agents only) that uses the new system before everyone.
Restore point (RP)A named, verified backup you can return to.

The safety block (inside every prompt)

commands
SAFETY (applies to everything below)
- Work on a NEW git branch off the current branch (name given below). Never push, merge, force-push or rewrite history.
- Never connect to or change production, and never run `bench migrate`, `bench restore`, `bench backup` or schema changes against any shared or live database. Database work only on a throwaway dev site or a restored COPY that you state in writing before touching it.
- Never print, log or commit secrets (passwords, tokens, site_config.json values, encryption_key). Use [REDACTED]; report key NAMES and paths only.
- Use fake data such as user@example.test. Do not copy customer or employee personal data into files.
- Do not claim anything works unless you ran it and saw it work; quote the command and redacted output. Label statements FACT, EVIDENCE, JUDGMENT or UNRESOLVED.
- Do NOT stop to ask for approval. If a human must do something (servers, DNS, certificates, production backups, secret storage, maintenance windows), write it under a heading USER-ACTION-REQUIRED in the phase document, mark the dependent checks UNVERIFIED with the exact command, and continue.
- Follow CLAUDE.md: tabs in Python, ruff config in pyproject.toml, small commits "type: summary", every patch idempotent and listed in patches.txt, update docs/PROGRESS.md.

Phase 1: Decide, measure and harden the current site

1. Goal, completion criteria and risks

Phase 1 at a glance

OutcomeYou know the real facts of today's database, backups are encrypted and a restore has been proven, and the decisions are written down
Claude Code does3 prompts: audit script, encrypted backup and restore, decision record and templates
You do11 steps: install age, take a backup copy, build a scratch copy, neutralise it, run queries, record, schedule backups, run a restore drill, confirm decisions
Exit testthe audit baseline is saved; one restore drill from an encrypted backup passed; ADR-008 accepted
Touches live?only a nightly backup job on the production host
Rollbackremove the cron line; revert code (the new options are off unless set)

What exactly happens in this phase: before and after

Nothing about the running system changes in this phase. You gain facts, encrypted backups and a proven restore. A concrete example: take one backup of a restored copy and compare.

Before Phase 1After Phase 1
A backup looks likea plain folder such as backups/20261105T020000Z-<site>/ holding *-database.sql.gz, file archives, SHA256SUMS, MANIFEST; the copy of the site config inside it contains the encryption_key (FACT: deploy/scripts/backup.sh header)with NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT set, a single file backups/20261105T020000Z-<site>.tar.age, unreadable without the private key. With NXERP_BACKUP_DELETE_PLAINTEXT=1 the plain folder is removed
Restoringworks from a plain folder; no drill has ever been recordedworks from the .tar.age file; one drill done on a scratch copy, with the time it took written down
What we know about the databasethe claims in Part 1 are from reading codemeasured on a restored copy: which apps' tables are in the one database, and what the one login may do (saved in docs/architecture-isolation/measurements.md)
Containersmay gain extra privilegessecurity_opt: no-new-privileges on the shared anchor of deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml
Decisionsassumptions A1 to A9 openeach confirmed or changed in docs/adr/ADR-008-application-isolation.md
What users seenothing changes

How it works in the code (walk-through)

  1. deploy/scripts/backup.sh (existing) runs the site backup and verifies it (gzip -t, table count, tar -t, SHA256SUMS).
  2. NEW branch in the same script: if NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT is set, it runs tar -C <dir> -cf - . | age -r "$NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT" and writes <dir>.tar.age plus its SHA-256.
  3. deploy/scripts/restore.sh (existing) now accepts a .tar.age: it needs NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_IDENTITY (the private key file), decrypts into a mode-700 temporary folder, verifies SHA256SUMS, then runs its existing steps (safety backup, maintenance mode, bench restore, health check) and removes the temporary folder.
  4. NEW scripts/isolation_audit.sh uses the helpers in deploy/scripts/lib.sh (inbench, dc) to run SQL as the site's own database login and to list container environments and published ports.
  5. NEW documents record the result: docs/architecture-isolation/measurements.md and docs/adr/ADR-008-application-isolation.md.

Goal: turn the unverified parts of Part 1 into measured facts, record the owner decisions, and remove the cheap exposures on the stack that exists today. No architecture change yet.

Done whenEvidence
Decisions A1 to A7 are confirmed or changed in docs/adr/ADR-008-application-isolation.md NEWADR status changes from Proposed to Accepted by the owner
Appendix queries U1 to U5 have been run on a restored copy and the redacted output sits in docs/architecture-isolation/measurements.md NEWtable filled, no secrets
Backups are encrypted with age; a restore drill from an encrypted backup passeddrill log with timings
A nightly backup runs on the production hostcrontab -l line and a first encrypted file
scripts/isolation_audit.sh NEW exists and its baseline output on today's single site is recordedPASS/FAIL table

Risks: a restored production copy puts personal data on a machine (encrypt the disk, delete afterwards); losing the age private key makes every backup unreadable (keep two offline copies); a backup taken at peak hours slows users (run off-peak).

3. What I must do myselfYou

These steps use the existing stack in deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml (the "old stack"). Replace <...> placeholders. Run commands from the repository root unless stated.

Step 1.1 Check Docker works

Docker runs the stack. You need Docker Desktop (Windows or macOS) or Docker Engine (Linux), running.

commands
docker version
docker compose version
Expectedboth print a client and server version with no error.Checkdocker ps prints a header line.Undonothing to undo.

Step 1.2 Install age and make the backup key pair

age encrypts a file so only the holder of the private key can open it.

commands
# Linux (Debian/Ubuntu):   sudo apt install age
# macOS:                   brew install age
# Windows:                 winget search age   (install the entry from FiloSottile), or scoop install age
age --version
age-keygen -o nxerp-backup.key
Expectedage-keygen prints Public key: age1.... The file nxerp-backup.key holds the private key.Checkage --version prints a version.Do nowcopy nxerp-backup.key to two offline places (an encrypted USB stick and a password manager attachment) and then delete it from the working folder. Write the age1... public key into your notes: this is <age-public-key>.Undoyou cannot undo key loss.Warningif every copy of the private key is lost, every backup encrypted with it is permanently unreadable.

Step 1.3 Take a production backup copy (read-only on the data, but it loads the server)

A backup is a copy of the database and files. Run it off-peak. This is the only step that touches the production host, and it only reads data.

commands
# on the production host, in the deployment directory (for example /opt/nxerp)
NXERP_ENV_FILES=.env NXERP_BACKUP_DIR=/var/backups/nxerp deploy/scripts/backup.sh
Expectedthe last line printed is a directory such as /var/backups/nxerp/<UTC stamp>-<site>.Checkthe directory holds *-database.sql.gz, file archives, SHA256SUMS, MANIFEST. After Phase 1's code is merged you can instead set NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT=<age-public-key> to get an encrypted .tar.age. Copy it to the scratch machine encrypted in transit: scp -r <user>@<prod-host>:/var/backups/nxerp/<dir> ./scratch-backup/.Undodelete the backup directory when finished (rm -rf). It contains personal data and encryption_key; keep it only on an encrypted disk.

Step 1.4 Build a scratch copy of the old stack

This is a separate, disposable copy of the stack (project name nxerp-scratch) on your scratch machine, with its own database. It never talks to production.

commands
cp deploy/env/staging-like/.env.example deploy/env/staging-like/.env
# edit .env: set NXERP_IMAGE_TAG to the tag you run in production, NXERP_SITE=<production site name>,
# and generate NXERP_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD and NXERP_ADMIN_PASSWORD with:
python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(24))'
chmod 600 deploy/env/staging-like/.env

export NXERP_COMPOSE_PROJECT=nxerp-scratch NXERP_ENV_FILES=deploy/env/staging-like/.env NXERP_HTTP_PORT=18080
docker compose -p nxerp-scratch --env-file deploy/env/staging-like/.env -f deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml up -d mariadb redis-cache redis-queue configurator
docker compose -p nxerp-scratch --env-file deploy/env/staging-like/.env -f deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml --profile init run --rm create-site
docker compose -p nxerp-scratch --env-file deploy/env/staging-like/.env -f deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml up -d
Expectedcreate-site ends without error; docker compose -p nxerp-scratch ps shows the services running.Checkcurl -s http://localhost:18080/api/method/ping prints {"message":"pong"}.Undodocker compose -p nxerp-scratch down -v (this deletes the scratch data, which is the point).

Step 1.5 Restore the production copy into the scratch stack

commands
NXERP_SITE=<production site name> NXERP_COMPOSE_PROJECT=nxerp-scratch NXERP_ENV_FILES=deploy/env/staging-like/.env \
  deploy/scripts/restore.sh --yes ./scratch-backup/<dir>
Expectedthe script verifies checksums, takes a safety backup, restores, and runs a health check.Checkit exits 0. If encrypted passwords do not decrypt afterwards, copy the backup's encryption_key into the scratch site (this puts a secret in the container's process list on a scratch machine only):
commands
docker compose -p nxerp-scratch --env-file deploy/env/staging-like/.env -f deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml \
  cp ./scratch-backup/<dir>/<stamp>-<site>-site_config_backup.json backend:/tmp/site_config_backup.json
docker compose -p nxerp-scratch --env-file deploy/env/staging-like/.env -f deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml \
  exec -T backend bash -lc 'cd /home/frappe/frappe-bench && key=$(python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open(\"/tmp/site_config_backup.json\"))[\"encryption_key\"])") && bench --site <production site name> set-config encryption_key "$key" && rm /tmp/site_config_backup.json'

Undo: docker compose -p nxerp-scratch down -v and re-run Step 1.4.

Step 1.6 Neutralise the scratch copy so it cannot contact real people

A restored copy still holds real email settings and webhooks. Without this step it could email customers or call external systems.

commands
S="docker compose -p nxerp-scratch --env-file deploy/env/staging-like/.env -f deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml exec -T backend bash -lc"
$S 'cd /home/frappe/frappe-bench && bench --site <site> set-config mute_emails 1 && bench --site <site> disable-scheduler'
$S 'cd /home/frappe/frappe-bench && bench --site <site> mariadb' <<'SQL'
UPDATE `tabEmail Account` SET enable_incoming=0, enable_outgoing=0;
UPDATE tabWebhook SET enabled=0;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS active_email_accounts FROM `tabEmail Account` WHERE enable_incoming=1 OR enable_outgoing=1;
SQL
Expectedthe last query prints 0.Checksame.Undodiscard the scratch copy; never re-enable on it. (UNRESOLVED: bench ... mariadb needs the MariaDB client in the image; if the command fails, run the SQL with docker compose -p nxerp-scratch exec -T mariadb mariadb -uroot using MYSQL_PWD set from your env file.)

Step 1.7 Run the measurement queries (Appendix U2 to U5) and record them

Run each query in the appendix against the scratch copy and paste the redacted output into docs/architecture-isolation/measurements.md. State at the top: "Database touched: scratch copy of production backup <stamp>, project nxerp-scratch". Replace real names with placeholders, for example [Customer Name].

Expecteda table of DocTypes per app, cross-app Link counts, the single per-site account with one ALL PRIVILEGES grant on its own database.Checkthe grant line has no *.*, no GRANT OPTION, and a host that is not % (if it is %, write that down: it is a finding).Undonothing changes in the database.

Step 1.8 Record the baseline isolation result

commands
NXERP_SITE=<site> NXERP_COMPOSE_PROJECT=nxerp-scratch NXERP_ENV_FILES=deploy/env/staging-like/.env scripts/isolation_audit.sh all
Expectedgrants shows one account for all six apps (the problem, measured); root-env PASS; ports PASS (only the proxy publishes).Checksave the output in measurements.md.Undonone.

Step 1.9 Schedule the nightly encrypted backup on the production host

commands
crontab -e
# add one line (the host's own scheduler; 02:15 every night):
15 2 * * * cd /opt/nxerp && NXERP_ENV_FILES=.env NXERP_BACKUP_DIR=/var/backups/nxerp NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT=<age-public-key> NXERP_BACKUP_DELETE_PLAINTEXT=1 NXERP_BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS=30 deploy/scripts/backup.sh >> /var/log/nxerp-backup.log 2>&1
Expectedtomorrow /var/backups/nxerp holds a .tar.age and no plaintext directory.Checkls -l /var/backups/nxerp and tail /var/log/nxerp-backup.log. Copy backups off the host (set NXERP_BACKUP_UPLOAD_CMD, for example an rclone wrapper; the choice of storage is yours).Undocrontab -e and delete the line.

Step 1.10 Run a restore drill from an encrypted backup

commands
NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_IDENTITY=./nxerp-backup.key NXERP_SITE=<site> NXERP_COMPOSE_PROJECT=nxerp-scratch \
  NXERP_ENV_FILES=deploy/env/staging-like/.env deploy/scripts/restore.sh --yes ./scratch-backup/<dir>.tar.age
deploy/scripts/healthcheck.sh
Expectedrestore exit 0 and health pass. Write down how long it took: that is your real recovery time.Undodocker compose -p nxerp-scratch down -v.

Step 1.11 Confirm the decisions

Open docs/adr/ADR-008-application-isolation.md, and for each of A1 to A7 write "confirmed" or your change. Record the hosting and data-classification decisions in the same file. Check: status set to Accepted by you. Undo: edit the ADR.

Step 2.9 Prove the template with three throwaway apps (recommended)

This proves that apps 3 to 5 can join with no change to anything else. The stand-ins are empty (only the platform gate is installed), named app3, app4, app5, and are deleted afterwards. They are never shown to users and no HRMS, Project Management or Budget software is installed.

commands
for n in app3 app4 app5; do cp deploy/env/isolated/app.env.example deploy/env/isolated/$n.env; chmod 600 deploy/env/isolated/$n.env; done
# edit each file: NXERP_SITE=$n.<domain>, NXERP_STACK_APPS=nxerp, fresh passwords,
# NXERP_DB_HOST/NXERP_DB_NETWORK: standard for app3 and app4, restricted for app5
printf 'app3 app3 standard\napp4 app4 standard\napp5 app5 restricted\n' >> deploy/env/isolated/stacks.list
for n in app3 app4 app5; do deploy/scripts/stack.sh $n create-site; deploy/scripts/stack.sh $n up; done
deploy/scripts/edge-gen.sh && deploy/scripts/stack.sh edge up
scripts/isolation_audit.sh all
Expectedsix sites answer pong; the audit shows every login denied on every other database (the 6 by 6 matrix in Section 2.5).Checkdocker ps shows about 39 long-running containers (see the footprint table in 2.8).Undofor n in app3 app4 app5; do NXERP_ALLOW_DESTROY=1 deploy/scripts/stack.sh $n down -v; done, remove the three lines from deploy/env/isolated/stacks.list, delete the three env files, run deploy/scripts/edge-gen.sh and deploy/scripts/stack.sh edge up again.

8. Check it yourself, configuration, verification and rollback

Check it yourself: before and after

Do each before check first on the scratch copy (Phase 1 steps 1.4 to 1.6) and write the result down, then run the after check. Nothing here touches production.

Check 1.1 A backup is encrypted

commands
ls backups/*/                                  # the BEFORE view: plain files
NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT=<age-public-key> NXERP_BACKUP_DELETE_PLAINTEXT=1 deploy/scripts/backup.sh
ls backups/
Beforea folder containing *-database.sql.gz and site_config_backup.json.Afterone <stamp>-<site>.tar.age file and no plain folder.Checkthe last line the script prints is the .tar.age path.

Check 1.2 The wrong key cannot open it

commands
age-keygen -o wrong.key
age -d -i wrong.key backups/<stamp>-<site>.tar.age > /dev/null
Expectedan error that no identity matched, and no output file content.Undorm wrong.key.

Check 1.3 A restore from the encrypted backup works

commands
NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_IDENTITY=./nxerp-backup.key NXERP_SITE=<site> NXERP_COMPOSE_PROJECT=nxerp-scratch \
  NXERP_ENV_FILES=deploy/env/staging-like/.env deploy/scripts/restore.sh --yes backups/<stamp>-<site>.tar.age
deploy/scripts/healthcheck.sh
Expectedthe restore exits 0 and the health check passes.Checkwrite down how long it took.Undodocker compose -p nxerp-scratch down -v.

Check 1.4 See the shared database for yourself (the "before picture" for the whole project)

Run SQL blocks U3 and U4 from the appendix on the scratch copy.

ExpectedU3 lists several apps (for example erpnext, helpdesk, frappe) inside this one database, and U4 shows one login with ALL PRIVILEGES on that one database.Checksave both outputs in measurements.md. After Phase 5 the same queries on each new database show one app only.

Check 1.5 Containers are not carrying the database root password

commands
NXERP_SITE=<site> NXERP_COMPOSE_PROJECT=nxerp-scratch NXERP_ENV_FILES=deploy/env/staging-like/.env scripts/isolation_audit.sh root-env
docker inspect <backend container> --format '{{.HostConfig.SecurityOpt}}'
ExpectedPASS for backend, websocket, queue-worker and scheduler, and [no-new-privileges:true]. Pass rule for the phase: checks 1.1 to 1.5 recorded, one restore drill passed, ADR-008 confirmed.

Configuration, verification and rollback

Config and infrastructure: new env variable names NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT, NXERP_BACKUP_AGE_IDENTITY, NXERP_BACKUP_DELETE_PLAINTEXT; a cron entry on the production host; an age key pair held offline; a scratch Docker project nxerp-scratch. How to verify the phase worked: bash -n and shellcheck clean; an encrypted backup exists and a restore drill from it passed; measurements.md has real outputs; scripts/isolation_audit.sh all output recorded; ADR-008 Accepted. How to roll back: revert the commits (code only); remove the cron line; plaintext backups continue to work because the new variables are optional. Reverting code does not reverse database changes; this phase makes none.

Phase 2: Stack template, database tiers and network boundaries

1. Goal, completion criteria and risks

Phase 2 at a glance

OutcomeThree empty, separate sites (identity, ERPNext, Helpdesk), two database servers, private networks and one edge proxy exist and pass the isolation tests
Claude Code does3 prompts: database servers and networks; the app stack template and stack.sh; edge proxy, isolation tests and docs
You do9 steps: DNS, firewall, certificates, secret files, start database servers, create sites, start the edge, run tests T1 to T6, prove the template with three throwaway apps
Exit testT1 to T6 pass on the new environments and on three throwaway stand-in apps made from the template; the old stack still passes healthcheck.sh
Touches live?no: the new environments are empty and run beside the old one
Rollbackstop the new projects; remove DNS records

What exactly happens in this phase: before and after

You build the new separate environments next to the old one, with no data in them. The live system is not touched. A concrete example: ask Helpdesk's database login to read an ERPNext table.

Before Phase 2 (the old stack)After Phase 2 (the new stacks, empty)
Containers8 in one project: backend, websocket, queue-worker, scheduler, redis-cache, redis-queue, mariadb, proxy (FACT: deploy/docker/compose/staging-like/compose.yaml)the old project unchanged, plus projects nxerp-db (2 MariaDB), nxerp-id, nxerp-erp, nxerp-hd (6 containers each) and nxerp-edge (1)
Databasesone app databasethree empty ones: identity and Helpdesk on the standard server, ERPNext on the restricted server
Database loginsonethree, plus the admin password used only inside the one-time create-site run
Redisone cache and one queueone pair per site
Networksnone definednxerp-db-standard and nxerp-db-restricted (internal, no internet), nxerp-api, one private network per stack
Open portsthe proxy on 8080only the edge proxy, on 127.0.0.1 (the host proxy faces the internet)
Example: read tabCustomer as Helpdesk's loginworks: it is the same database (returns a number)ERROR 1142 or 1044, denied: that database is not even visible
Adding another appwould mean touching shared thingsone env file plus one line in deploy/env/isolated/stacks.list, then stack.sh <name> create-site

How it works in the code (walk-through)

  1. deploy/scripts/stack.sh hd create-site NEW sets NXERP_COMPOSE_FILE, NXERP_COMPOSE_PROJECT=nxerp-hd, NXERP_ENV_FILES=deploy/env/isolated/hd.env and calls the one-time create-site service in deploy/docker/compose/isolated/stack.compose.yaml NEW, the only place the database admin password is given.
  2. That service runs bench new-site ... --mariadb-user-host-login-scope "$NXERP_DB_USER_SCOPE". Frappe's own setup_database then runs CREATE USER, CREATE DATABASE and GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON <db>.* for that one site (EVIDENCE: frappe/database/db_manager.py).
  3. The same service installs only the apps in NXERP_STACK_APPS (for Helpdesk: telephony helpdesk nxerp) and runs bench use.
  4. The stack file attaches the database containers to the internal network nxerp-db-standard (or -restricted) and gives the backend a unique name on nxerp-api (for example hd-backend), so no stack can see another stack's Redis or database.
  5. deploy/scripts/edge-gen.sh NEW reads stacks.list and writes the edge proxy configuration and its network list; stack.sh edge up starts it.
  6. scripts/isolation_audit.sh NEW proves the walls: cross-database read and write, network reach, root password, published ports.

Goal: stand up three empty stacks (id, erp, hd), two MariaDB instances (standard and restricted) and one edge proxy, so the isolation controls can be tested before any data moves. The old stack keeps running untouched.

Done whenEvidence
Each stack has its own site, database, database account, Redis and secrets volumedeploy/scripts/stack.sh <stack> bench list-apps per stack; docker volume ls shows one sites volume per project
erp is on the restricted instance; id and hd share the standard instance with separate accountsdocker ps shows two MariaDB containers; Appendix U4 per stack
Tests T1 to T6 passmeasurements.md section "Phase 2 tests" with outputs
Three throwaway stand-in apps (app3 to app5) made from the template pass the same tests, then are removedisolation_audit.sh all output for six sites
https://id.<domain>, erp.<domain>, hd.<domain> each answer pingcurl outputs
The old stack is unchanged and healthydeploy/scripts/healthcheck.sh against it

Risks: Docker adds each service name as an alias on every network it joins, so identical names (backend) on a shared network collide: the stack file must give unique aliases (the prompt says how). One image serving three stacks is assumed (Appendix U12): if Frappe loads an app's hooks on a site that does not have it installed, a build change is needed. A host-scoped database account depends on the Docker subnet you choose.

3. What I must do myselfYou

Assumes Phase 1 is done and Phase 2's files are merged. Replace <domain> with your real domain, for example example.test in documentation.

Step 2.1 Create DNS records

DNS maps names to IP addresses. You need three names pointing at the server that will run the stacks.

commands
# at your DNS provider's control panel, create three A records:
id.<domain>   A   <server public IP>
erp.<domain>  A   <server public IP>
hd.<domain>   A   <server public IP>
# then check from your own machine:
nslookup id.<domain>
nslookup erp.<domain>
nslookup hd.<domain>
Expectedeach answers with your server IP (it can take minutes to hours).Checksame.Undodelete the three records.

Step 2.2 Open only the ports that are needed

A firewall decides which network ports the outside world can reach. Only web ports should be open. Warning: allow SSH first, or you will lock yourself out.

commands
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status
Expectedstatus lists only 22, 80, 443.Checkfrom another machine, nc -zv <server IP> 3306 fails.Undosudo ufw disable. (Docker publishes ports around ufw, which is why the edge binds to 127.0.0.1 only and the host proxy in the next step is the public entry.)

Step 2.3 Install the host reverse proxy and certificates

HTTPS needs a certificate. certbot obtains free ones from Let's Encrypt. The host's nginx receives public traffic and forwards it to the edge container on 127.0.0.1:8080.

commands
sudo apt install nginx certbot python3-certbot-nginx
sudo tee /etc/nginx/sites-available/nxerp >/dev/null <<'EOF'
server {
  listen 80;
  server_name id.<domain> erp.<domain> hd.<domain>;
  client_max_body_size 50m;
  location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_read_timeout 120s;
  }
}
EOF
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/nxerp /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/nxerp
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
sudo certbot --nginx -d id.<domain> -d erp.<domain> -d hd.<domain>

Step 2.4 Create the secret files

Each stack gets its own passwords. Never reuse one password for two stacks. These files stay on the server and are never committed.

commands

python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(24))'    # run once per CHANGE_ME value; paste into the file
git check-ignore -v deploy/env/isolated/db.env

Fill: edge.env gets NXERP_DOMAIN=<domain> and NXERP_EDGE_PORT=8080; db.env gets the two root passwords (standard and restricted); each stack file gets its own NXERP_ADMIN_PASSWORD, site name (id.<domain> and so on), NXERP_DB_HOST, NXERP_DB_NETWORK, NXERP_DB_USER_SCOPE (172.30.10.% for id and hd, 172.30.20.% for erp), NXERP_STACK_APPS (nxerp for id; payments erpnext nxerp for erp; telephony helpdesk nxerp for hd), and NXERP_IMAGE_TAG (the tag you run today).

Expectedgit check-ignore -v prints the matching ignore rule.Checkls -l deploy/env/isolated shows -rw-------.Undodelete the filled files and regenerate (before any site exists; after a site exists changing a password needs the rotation procedure).

Configuration, verification and rollback

Config and infrastructure: three DNS records; host firewall; host nginx plus certificates; Docker networks nxerp-db-standard, nxerp-db-restricted, nxerp-api; compose projects nxerp-db, nxerp-id, nxerp-erp, nxerp-hd, nxerp-edge; env files under deploy/env/isolated/ (git-ignored, mode 600). How to verify the phase worked: list-apps per stack matches the expected list; T1 to T6 pass; docker ps shows one published port (loopback edge); the old stack still passes deploy/scripts/healthcheck.sh. How to roll back: deploy/scripts/stack.sh edge down, then each stack and the DB tier down (without -v they keep data, which is empty anyway); remove DNS records and the host nginx file if you abandon the plan. The old stack never changed, so users are unaffected. Reverting the code does not delete Docker volumes or networks: remove them with docker volume rm and docker network rm after confirming they hold no data you need.

Phase 3: Identity site and login federation

1. Goal, completion criteria and risks

Phase 3 at a glance

OutcomeThe user signs in once at the identity site; the app sites accept that login; an access grant given on the identity site reaches the app site; the existing gate keeps enforcing on each site
Claude Code does4 prompts: a spike that proves the login flow; registry, routing and login page; grant provisioning; setup helpers, docs and lockout safety
You do9 steps: read the spike, set site roles, service users and keys, register app sites, OAuth clients, Social Login Keys, test SSO, switch off local login last, test revocation
Exit testT7 and T8 pass on staging; the existing nxerp tests pass with the new setting unset; the 35 hostile redirect payloads plus new ones are still refused
Touches live?no: staging only, and everything is off unless nxerp_site_role is set
Rollbackunset nxerp_site_role; re-enable local login; revert code

What exactly happens in this phase: before and after

Still staging only. Every new behaviour is off unless the site setting nxerp_site_role is set, so merging the code changes nothing on the live system. A concrete example: a new support agent, user@example.test.

Before Phase 3After Phase 3 (staging, setting on)
Where you type your password/login on the one site/login on id.<domain> only. App sites show a single "Sign in with NXERP" button
Where the agent existsone User row on the one site, with their rolesthe master User on the identity site, and a copy (no password) in the Helpdesk site's own database, created by provisioning
Giving Helpdesk accesstick the role NXERP Access: Helpdesk on the user; effective at oncetick it on the identity site; it reaches Helpdesk within about a minute; a nightly check repairs differences
Taking access awayuntick the roleuntick on the identity site; the user is disabled on Helpdesk within about a minute
Launcher tilessame-site paths such as /helpdesk/homeon the identity site, each tile links to that app's own address
Redirect safety (routing.safe_target)refuses every address that has a hoststill refuses everything except exact addresses registered for an app
Setting offn/anxerp_site_role unset: the platform behaves exactly as before

How it works in the code (walk-through)

  1. An administrator ticks the role. The grant API nxerp.api.access.set_app_access (apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/api/access.py, line 53) saves the user, and on an identity site also enqueues provisioning.
  2. The User document event on_update in apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/hooks.py calls NEW nxerp.federation.outbox.on_user_change. It writes one row in the identity database table NXERP Provisioning Outbox (user, app, Enable or Disable, status Pending, a unique idempotency key). Only runs when nxerp_site_role is identity.
  3. The scheduler runs nxerp.federation.outbox.process. For each pending row it reads the app's NXERP Peer record (address, token) and sends POST nxerp.federation.api.provision_user with Authorization: token <key>:<secret> and the header X-Frappe-Site-Name.
  4. On the app site, provision_user (NEW, apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/federation/api.py) requires the role NXERP Provisioner. It creates or enables the user with no password, adds only the role NXERP Access: <this app>, and refuses Administrator, Guest and any attempt to grant System Manager. Every denial is logged by apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/audit.py.
  5. When the agent opens Helpdesk, the app's Social Login Key (provider Frappe) sends the browser to the identity site's frappe.integrations.oauth2.authorize. After the password and 2FA, the app exchanges the one-time code (get_token), asks openid_profile who it is, and signs in the matching, enabled user, else shows the "no access" page.
  6. /nxerp/go (apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/www/nxerp/go.py) sends the user on, using registry.allowed_origins() so only registered app addresses are accepted.
  7. Every night nxerp.federation.reconcile.run compares both user lists and fixes differences toward the identity site.

Goal: the user signs in once at the identity site id; the app sites accept that login; grants given on id reach the app sites; the existing gate keeps enforcing on each site. Everything is off by default: a site without the new setting nxerp_site_role behaves exactly as today, so merging the code changes nothing on the live stack.

Done whenEvidence
A spike document records what Frappe v16.53.0 really does for the OAuth flow, userinfo, sign-up policy and role claimsdocs/architecture-isolation/spike-federation.md NEW with commands and redacted outputs
All existing nxerp tests still pass on a site without nxerp_site_rolebench --site <dev-site> run-tests --app nxerp output
New tests pass: provisioning, deprovisioning, reconcile, token scope, origin allowlisttest_federation.py, extended test_routing.py, test_registry.py
On staging: login at id, open hd with no second prompt; revoke on id disables the user on hd; direct password login on hd refusedtests T7 and T8
The 35 hostile redirect payloads in test_routing.py are still refused, plus new cross-origin casestest output

Risks: open redirect through the origin allowlist; lockout when local login is disabled before SSO works; drift between id and app users; the userinfo-only flow (no JWKS) and role mapping are unproven until the spike.

Phase 4: ERP bridge and Helpdesk decoupling

1. Goal, completion criteria and risks

Phase 4 at a glance

OutcomeHelpdesk reads customer details from ERPNext through a versioned read-only API and keeps its customer mirror current from signed change events; Helpdesk no longer writes to ERPNext
Claude Code does3 prompts: ERPNext side (API and webhooks installer); Helpdesk side (mode switch, client, receiver); contract, screen and docs
You do6 steps: confirm the policy, reader service user, receiver service user and webhooks, switch bridge mode on in staging, test with a fake customer, run T9 and T10
Exit testT9 and T10 pass; both test suites pass with the mode unset; the fake-customer test passes with it set
Touches live?no: staging only, and everything is off unless nxerp_bridge_mode is set
Rollbackunset nxerp_bridge_mode (old behaviour returns, because the old code is kept until Phase 5); disable the webhooks

What exactly happens in this phase: before and after

Staging only, behind the setting nxerp_bridge_mode (unset = today's behaviour, because the old code is kept until Phase 5). A concrete example: a customer called "Fake Customer One".

Before Phase 4 (setting off, today)After Phase 4 (setting on)
Create the customer in ERPNextan in-process hook (apps/helpdesk/helpdesk/integrations/erpnext/customer.py, after_insert) creates the HD Customer straight away, because both live in one databaseERPNext sends a signed message (webhook); Helpdesk verifies it and creates or updates its own HD Customer within about a minute
Edit the customer type in Helpdeskthe change is copied into ERPNext's Customer (apps/helpdesk/helpdesk/integrations/erpnext/utils.py)nothing is written to ERPNext
Delete the HD Customerthe linked ERPNext Customer is deleted too (hd_customer.py, on_trash)nothing happens to ERPNext
Delete the ERPNext Customerthe linked HD Customer is deleted (customer.py, on_trash)the HD Customer stays, its link is cleared, and a comment explains why
Customer details on a ticketnot shown live from ERPNexta small panel from a read-only API call, cached for 5 minutes; if ERPNext is down the ticket still opens with the name
Permissions copied between appsUser Permission and DocShare rows are mirrored both waysnot mirrored; each app uses its own grants
A custom field on ERPNext's CustomerHelpdesk adds Customer.hd_customernot needed in bridge mode

How it works in the code (walk-through)

  1. Announce (ERPNext side). nxerp.bridge.setup.install_customer_webhooks (NEW, apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/bridge/setup.py) creates three Webhook records on Customer (after insert, on update, on trash) with signing on. The platform app does this without importing ERPNext.
  2. Receive (Helpdesk side). The webhook calls NEW helpdesk.integrations.erpnext.events.receive_customer_event (apps/helpdesk/helpdesk/integrations/erpnext/events.py). It first verifies the HMAC-SHA256 signature, rejects bodies over 64 KB, and is idempotent on (customer, modified). Only then does it touch HD Customer.
  3. Safety net. run_daily_pull (same file) calls the provider's list_customers once a day and repairs anything a lost message missed.
  4. Read details. When a ticket opens, NEW bridge_client.py asks GET nxerp.bridge.v1.customer_context on the ERPNext site (apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/bridge/v1.py). The provider checks the token's role (NXERP Bridge Reader), applies a rate limit, writes an audit line, and returns a small answer: name, type, group, territory, disabled, open invoice count. No amounts and no addresses.
  5. The switch. In bridge mode should_sync() in apps/helpdesk/helpdesk/integrations/erpnext/utils.py returns false, so every old hook becomes a no-op. The old code is deleted only in Phase 5 after decision point D.

Goal: Helpdesk reads customer context from ERPNext through a versioned, read-only API and keeps its HD Customer mirror up to date from signed events. Helpdesk stops writing into ERPNext. The old in-process sync keeps working on the live single-site stack until the cutover (the new behaviour is behind nxerp_bridge_mode).

Done whenEvidence
The contract bridge-v1 is written down and covered by contract tests on both sidesdocs/architecture/bridge-v1.md NEW, test_bridge.py, test_bridge_client.py
With nxerp_bridge_mode unset the Helpdesk suite behaves as before (577 tests were passing at last run: FACT from docs/PROGRESS.md)Helpdesk test output
With it set: a new, changed, renamed and deleted ERP customer reaches hd; Helpdesk never writes to Customertests on a two-site dev bench
T9 and T10 passoutputs

Risks: the sync would silently stop if should_sync() is not replaced (it tests "ERPNext installed on this site"); webhook delivery is not guaranteed (3 tries, then only logged), so a nightly pull is mandatory; the DTO's ERPNext field names must be checked against the pinned ERPNext; losing the write path changes what support teams can do (owner decision A3).

Step 4.3 Create the receiver service user on hd and install the webhooks on erp

The webhook is a message ERPNext posts to Helpdesk when a customer changes. It carries a signature so Helpdesk can reject forgeries.

  1. On hd create svc-erp@<domain> with role NXERP Bridge Receiver only; generate keys; save the secret.
  2. Generate a shared signing secret: python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))'. On hd, put it in the Peer record erpnext field "Webhook Secret".
  3. Install the three webhooks on erp (the helper reads secrets from the environment, so they do not enter the command line):
commands
export NXERP_BRIDGE_RECEIVER_URL='http://hd-backend:8000/api/method/helpdesk.integrations.erpnext.events.receive_customer_event'
export NXERP_BRIDGE_WEBHOOK_SECRET='<signing secret>'
export NXERP_BRIDGE_RECEIVER_TOKEN='<svc-erp api key>:<svc-erp api secret>'
docker compose -p nxerp-erp --env-file deploy/env/isolated/erp.env -f deploy/docker/compose/isolated/stack.compose.yaml \
  exec -T -e NXERP_BRIDGE_RECEIVER_URL -e NXERP_BRIDGE_WEBHOOK_SECRET -e NXERP_BRIDGE_RECEIVER_TOKEN backend \
  bash -lc 'cd /home/frappe/frappe-bench && bench --site erp.<domain> execute nxerp.bridge.setup.install_customer_webhooks'
unset NXERP_BRIDGE_WEBHOOK_SECRET NXERP_BRIDGE_RECEIVER_TOKEN

Configuration, verification and rollback

Config and infrastructure: site config nxerp_bridge_mode; Peer record erpnext on hd (internal URL, keys, webhook secret); service users svc-helpdesk (on erp) and svc-erp (on hd) with API keys; three Webhook records on erp; nxerp-api network (Phase 2). How to roll back: unset nxerp_bridge_mode on both sites (legacy behaviour returns because the legacy code and hooks were kept); disable the three Webhooks; disable the service users; revert the code. Phase 5: Migration, cutover, cleanup and the restricted database tier

1. Goal, completion criteria and risks

Phase 5 at a glance

OutcomeHelpdesk and identity run on the new sites with all existing data; ERPNext runs on its own database server; the old shared setup and the old in-process sync are retired
Claude Code does4 prompts: migration tools in Python; command line, ERP override and redirect rules; runbooks and workflows; retire the old sync code (separate branch, not merged until after D)
You do10 steps: rehearsal environment, two clean rehearsals, window preparation, cutover, canary, open to customers, 48-hour watch, decision point D, finalise and move ERP, abort path
Exit testtwo clean rehearsals; production reconciliation PASS; T1 to T6 on production; D recorded; ERP data restored on the restricted server
Touches live?yes: this is the only phase that does
Rollbackuntil D: unfreeze or delta export and import, point the edge back. After D: forward only

What exactly happens in this phase: before and after

This is the only phase that changes what people use. The numbers below are made-up examples to show what you compare; use your real counts.

Before the cutoverAfter the cutover
Addressesone host: /desk for ERPNext, /helpdesk for Helpdeskid.<domain> (login, launcher), erp.<domain>, hd.<domain>; old /helpdesk/... links answer 301 to hd.<domain>
Databasesone database with every app's tablesidentity database (users only), Helpdesk database (Helpdesk data), ERPNext database on the restricted server
Where Helpdesk's tables liveinside ERPNext's databasein Helpdesk's own database only (and removed from the old database after decision point D)
Tickets (example)Open 40, Replied 12, Closed 310the same 40, 12, 310
A ticket's messages and filesin the shared database and shared file areathe same messages and files, now in Helpdesk's own database and volume (proved by counts and file hashes)
Who signs in wherethe one siteid.<domain>, once
Backups and restoresthe whole systemone per database
The old systemlivestopped but kept for 30 days

How it works in the code (walk-through)

  1. deploy/scripts/cutover.sh freeze NEW puts the old site into maintenance mode, records and disables incoming mailboxes, waits for the outgoing mail queue to empty, and prints the freeze time T0.
  2. cutover.sh backup-source takes the verified backup RP0. cutover.sh clone-hd restores it into the new Helpdesk site, runs bench uninstall-app for ERPNext and payments, then nxerp.cutover.prune_helpdesk_site (NEW, apps/nxerp_platform/nxerp/cutover.py) removes core rows that belong only to ERP documents, reserves a ticket-number offset, migrates and rebuilds the search index.
  3. cutover.sh build-id runs identity_export on the old site and identity_import on the identity site: users, roles, password hashes and 2FA secrets, nothing else.
  4. cutover.sh reconcile compares per-record counts, name sets, file hashes and email message ids and prints PASS or FAIL.
  5. A canary of agents tries the new site, then mailbox polling and the customer portal are switched on at the new site only. Rolling back before decision point D uses delta-export and delta-import and leaves the old system intact.
  6. After D: cutover.sh finalize-erp removes Helpdesk from the old database (only if a verified RP-final exists), then cutover.sh move-erp restores the ERPNext data into the new ERPNext database on the restricted server.

Goal: move Helpdesk and the identity data out of the live site without losing or changing records, prove it twice on a restored copy first, cut over in a short freeze window, keep a real way back until a decision point, then clean up and put ERPNext on its own restricted database instance.

No personal data in the report.
   - reserve_naming_series_offset(offset): bump the HD Ticket naming series so new tickets on the new site cannot collide with the source after a rollback.
